nodes.body:
# Sprint Plan for AI-Native Autoscaling

## Phase 0: Workload Unification — Three-Level Canonical Model

**Goal:** Unify all workload generation through a single canonical spec format, retire legacy code paths, and set up the foundation for non-stationary workloads that autoscaling requires.

### Motivation

BLIS currently has three workload generation paths (CLI distribution-based, WorkloadSpec YAML, CSV trace replay) with ~300 lines of duplicated code across `sim/workload_config.go` and `sim/cluster/workload.go`. Features are scattered: rate stages are locked behind inference-perf, empirical PDFs behind ServeGen, multi-turn behind the reasoning block. These paths are mutually exclusive — you can't compose a ServeGen empirical distribution with inference-perf rate stages and multi-turn reasoning.

The unification introduces a **three-level canonical model** where every feature is composable, and external formats (ServeGen, inference-perf, GuideLLM, CSV traces) become **converters** that produce the canonical format.

### The Three-Level Model

```
Level 1: CLIENT POPULATION PROCESS — "Who is active, and when?"
│  Clients arrive and depart over time. Each client targets a specific model.
│  Non-stationary load is an emergent property of population dynamics:
│  diurnal = many arrivals at peak hours; spike = burst of arrivals;
│  scale-to-zero = all clients depart.
│
└─ Level 2: REQUEST GENERATION PROCESS — "How does this client produce requests?"
   │  Each active client generates requests at its own rate with its own
   │  token distributions, arrival process, prefix affinity, and modality.
   │
   └─ Level 3: CONVERSATION PROCESS — "How do turns within a request unfold?"
      Multi-turn sessions with think time, context accumulation,
      and reasoning token ratios.
```

### Canonical Spec Format (v2)

```yaml
version: "2"
seed: 42
horizon: 86400000000  # microseconds

# Level 1: Client population — two specification modes

# Mode A: Explicit clients with lifecycles (for controlled experiments, trace replay)
clients:
  - id: "web-user-1"
    model: "meta-llama/llama-3.1-8b-instruct"
    arrives_at_us: 0
    departs_at_us: 43200000000
    request_process:              # Level 2
      arrival: {process: "poisson", rate: 2.0}
      input_distribution: {type: "gaussian", params: {mean: 256, std_dev: 100, min: 10, max: 2048}}
      output_distribution: {type: "exponential", params: {mean: 128}}
      prefix_group: "system-prompt-v2"
      prefix_length: 256
      multimodal: ...             # optional
    conversation:                 # Level 3 (optional)
      multi_turn: {max_rounds: 3, think_time_us: 500000, context_growth: "accumulate"}
    slo_class: "interactive"
    streaming: true

# Mode B: Statistical cohorts (for generating realistic population dynamics)
cohorts:
  - name: "web-users"
    model: "meta-llama/llama-3.1-8b-instruct"
    count: 200
    arrival_process: {type: "poisson", rate: 50.0}  # client arrival rate
    session_duration: {type: "exponential", params: {mean: 1800000000}}  # ~30min
    diurnal:
      peak_hour: 14
      trough_hour: 4
      peak_trough_ratio: 5.0
    request_process:
      arrival: {process: "poisson", rate: 0.5}
      input_distribution: {type: "gaussian", params: {mean: 256, std_dev: 100, min: 10, max: 2048}}
      output_distribution: {type: "exponential", params: {mean: 128}}
    conversation:
      multi_turn: {max_rounds: 5, think_time_us: 500000, context_growth: "accumulate"}
    slo_class: "realtime"

  - name: "batch-jobs"
    model: "qwen/qwen-2.5-7b"
    count: 10
    arrival_process: {type: "constant", rate: 0.001}
    session_duration: {type: "constant", params: {value: 86400000000}}
    request_process:
      arrival: {process: "gamma", cv: 3.5, rate: 20.0}
      input_distribution: {type: "empirical", file: "production_input_pdf.json"}
      output_distribution: {type: "exponential", params: {mean: 512}}
```

### Converter Architecture

The simulator only parses the canonical format. External formats are supported through converters that produce canonical YAML:

```
  blis convert servegen ──────┐
  blis convert inference-perf ┼──► Canonical YAML ──► Simulator
  blis convert preset ────────┤    (one format)       (one parser)
  blis convert csv-trace ─────┤
  hand-written YAML ──────────┘
```

```bash
# Convert ServeGen traces → canonical spec
blis convert servegen /data/production/ -o workload.yaml

# Convert inference-perf config → canonical spec
blis convert inference-perf config.yaml -o workload.yaml

# Convert GuideLLM preset → canonical spec
blis convert preset chatbot --rate 100 --num-requests 500 -o workload.yaml

# Convert legacy CSV traces → canonical spec
blis convert csv-trace traces.csv -o workload.yaml

# Compose multiple sources (convenience helper)
blis compose \
  --from-servegen /data/production/:0.5 \
  --from-preset chatbot:0.3 \
  --from-spec spike-test.yaml:0.2 \
  -o combined.yaml
```

Composition happens at the YAML level — merge client/cohort lists, adjust rate fractions. Adding support for a new external format tomorrow is just a new `blis convert <format>` subcommand with zero changes to the spec or simulator.

### Supported Features (all composable on any client)

| Feature | Level | Available on any client |
|---------|-------|------------------------|
| Arrival process (Poisson, Gamma, Weibull, Constant) | 2 | Yes |
| Token distributions (Gaussian, Exponential, ParetoLogNormal, Empirical, Constant) | 2 | Yes |
| Multimodal (text, image, audio, video) | 2 | Yes |
| Prefix groups + prefix length | 2 | Yes |
| Multi-turn reasoning with context accumulation | 3 | Yes |
| SLO class / tenant ID | Client | Yes |
| Streaming mode | Client | Yes |
| Network model (RTT + bandwidth) | Client | Yes |
| Model affinity | Client | Yes |
| Client lifecycle (arrives/departs) | 1 | Yes |
| Diurnal population dynamics | 1 (cohorts) | Yes |
| Session duration distribution | 1 (cohorts) | Yes |

### What Gets Retired

- `GuideLLMConfig` struct and its 11-parameter constructor
- `sim/workload_config.go` — entire file (~170 lines of duplicated generation/CSV parsing)
- `sim/cluster/workload.go` — `generateRequestsFromDistribution()` and `generateRequestsFromCSV()` (~100 lines)
- The 4-way `if/else` in `cmd/root.go` for workload selection
- The placeholder `GuideLLMConfig` hack when using WorkloadSpec

### What Gets Added

- `"constant"` arrival process (deterministic fixed-rate, for GuideLLM backward compatibility)
- `model` field on clients (for multi-model autoscaling)
- `cohorts` specification mode (statistical population dynamics)
- `blis convert` subcommands (servegen, inference-perf, preset, csv-trace)
- `blis compose` convenience helper
- v1 → v2 spec migration (v1 specs still parse, auto-promoted internally)

### CLI Backward Compatibility

Existing CLI invocations continue to work — they internally synthesize a canonical spec:

| CLI Command | Internal Translation |
|-------------|---------------------|
| `blis run --rate 100 --prompt-tokens 512` | Single client, constant arrival, Gaussian distributions |
| `blis run --workload chatbot` | Single client from preset template |
| `blis run --workload traces --workload-traces-filepath X` | Explicit clients from CSV |
| `blis run --workload-spec X.yaml` | Direct parse (v1 or v2) |

***

## Phase 1A: Foundation — Make BLIS Dynamically Scalable

**Goal:** Extend the DES kernel so instances can be added/removed mid-simulation.

### Architecture Prerequisites
- [ ] Design doc: Instance lifecycle abstraction (`AddInstance`/`RemoveInstance` on `ClusterSimulator`)
  - Resolve fixed `[]*InstanceSimulator` slice → ID-indexed map or dynamic slice
  - `CachedSnapshotProvider` must handle instance arrival/departure
  - `pendingRequests` bookkeeping already uses string keys (robust)
  - Define instance states: `Provisioning → WarmingUp → Active → Draining → Terminated`
  - Scale-to-zero: relax `NumInstances >= 1` panic; define "cold start from zero" event sequence
- [ ] Design doc: Heterogeneous instance configuration
  - Per-instance `SimConfig` (different model, GPU, TP config per instance)
  - Extend `DeploymentConfig` → `[]InstanceConfig` or multiple `DeploymentConfig` objects
  - Routing implications: scorer weights may differ per-model (e.g., prefix-affinity irrelevant for some models)
  - Model-aware routing: requests with `model` field routed only to instances serving that model

### Core Autoscaler Module
- [ ] Design doc: Autoscaler subsystem module (per design guidelines §5.3)
  - Module contract: observes (metrics, queue depth, KV utilization), controls (instance count), owns (scaling state, cooldown timers), invariants (min ≤ replicas ≤ max, no scale during cooldown)
  - Event types: `AutoScaleCheckEvent`, `ScaleActionEvent`, `InstanceReadyEvent` (priority after routing/step/completion)
  - `AutoScalePolicy` interface (single-method: `Decide(AutoScaleContext) ScaleDecision`)
  - Strawman policies: `ThresholdScaler` (reactive), `PredictiveScaler` (trend-based), `Oscillator` (pathological control)
  - Actuation model: `ProvisioningDelay` (distribution), `WarmupProfile` (duration, cache cold-start penalty), `DrainPolicy` (immediate/wait/redirect)
  - Scale-to-zero: `DrainPolicy.DRAIN_ALL` + `MinReplicas=0`; cold-start-from-zero latency model
- [ ] Derive invariants:
  - INV-A1: `active_instances + provisioning_instances + draining_instances = total_managed_instances`
  - INV-A2: No routing to `Provisioning` or `Draining` instances
  - INV-A3: Scale-down must drain queue before terminating (or redirect in-flight)
- [ ] Derive hypotheses (pre-implementation, to validate post-implementation):
  - H-ScaleUp: Adding instance at ρ>0.8 reduces TTFT p99 by >30% within 2× provisioning_delay
  - H-ScaleDown: Removing instance at ρ<0.3 has <5% TTFT impact (headroom absorbs)
  - H-Oscillation: Naive threshold scaler with tight bounds produces scale oscillation (>3 scale events per 10× service_time)
  - H-WarmupCost: Cold instance with empty KV cache has >2× TTFT vs warm instance for first N requests
  - H-ScaleToZero: Cold-start-from-zero adds provisioning_delay + warmup_time to first request E2E
  - H-MultiModel: Model-aware routing with heterogeneous instances matches homogeneous per-model clusters within 10% TTFT

### Metrics & Observability Extensions
- [ ] New metrics: scaling_events_count, provisioning_latency_p99, instances_active (time-series), cost_proxy (instance-seconds), SLO_violation_rate
- [ ] Extend `ComputeFitness()` with cost and scaling-efficiency dimensions
- [ ] Extend counterfactual analysis: "what if we had scaled 30s earlier?"
- [ ] Trace records: `ScaleRecord` (already templated in extension-recipes.md)

### Macro Plan Derivation
- [ ] Derive PR sequence from the above design docs. Likely structure:
  - PR-W1: Workload unification — canonical spec v2, retire legacy paths, converters
  - PR-W2: Cohort-based population dynamics (non-stationary workloads)
  - PR-A1: Instance lifecycle (AddInstance/RemoveInstance + states + tests)
  - PR-A2: Autoscaler core (interface + ThresholdScaler + events + metrics)
  - PR-A3: Actuation model (provisioning delay, warmup, drain)
  - PR-A4: Heterogeneous instances + multi-model routing
  - PR-A5: Scale-to-zero support
  - PR-A6: Hypothesis experiments (H-ScaleUp through H-ScaleToZero)
- [ ] Validate llm-d/WVA alignment at each PR boundary
  - WPA (Workload-Proportional Autoscaling) maps to ThresholdScaler with utilization target
  - EPP (Endpoint Picker Policy) maps to existing composable scorer framework
  - Model routing maps to PR-A4 multi-model extension

***

## Phase 1B: Implementation Sprint

**Goal:** Land all PRs on an `autoscaling` feature branch.

- [ ] For each PR in the macro plan:
  - Run the PR workflow (micro-plan → convergence review → implement → code review → self-audit)
  - **Keep automated convergence rounds** (10 perspectives) — these catch real bugs every time
  - Skip the human gate at Step 3 (plan approval) for velocity — human reviews at branch merge instead
  - Merge into `autoscaling` branch (not `main`)
- [ ] Run hypothesis experiments (PR-A6) to validate autoscaler behavior
- [ ] Rebase `autoscaling` on `upstream/main`, resolve conflicts
- [ ] Full human review of the consolidated branch
- [ ] Merge into `main`

***

## Phase 1C: Evolutionary Algorithm Discovery

**Goal:** Use LLM-guided evolution to discover autoscaling algorithms that outperform hand-designed policies.

### Fitness Function Design
- [ ] Define the multi-objective fitness landscape:
  - **Latency**: TTFT p99, E2E p99 (from existing `ComputeFitness`)
  - **Cost**: total instance-seconds (minimize)
  - **SLO compliance**: fraction of requests meeting SLO target
  - **Stability**: scaling event frequency (penalize oscillation)
  - **Responsiveness**: time from overload detection to scale-up completion
- [ ] Define behavioral feature dimensions for MAP-Elites ([OpenEvolve](https://github.com/algorithmicsuperintelligence/openevolve)):
  - Workload regime (steady/bursty/diurnal)
  - Scale range (2-4 instances vs 4-16 vs 16-64)
  - Model mix (single-model vs multi-model)

### OpenEvolve Integration — Algorithm Structure Discovery
- [ ] Design the evolvable program template:
  - The `AutoScalePolicy.Decide()` method body is the evolved code
  - `AutoScaleContext` (signals) is the fixed input interface
  - `ScaleDecision` is the fixed output interface
  - BLIS simulation is the fitness evaluator (deterministic, fast, no GPU needed)
- [ ] Configure OpenEvolve:
  - Sandbox: BLIS binary execution (CPU-only, ~seconds per evaluation)
  - Evaluation suite: N workload scenarios (steady, burst, diurnal, spike, scale-to-zero recovery)
  - Seeds: multiple seeds per scenario for determinism validation (INV-6)
  - Quality-diversity: MAP-Elites over (workload_regime × scale_range) feature space
- [ ] Run evolution campaigns, collect Pareto-optimal algorithm set

### GEPA Integration — Parameter Tuning
- [ ] Implement `GEPAAdapter` for BLIS:
  - `evaluate()`: run BLIS with candidate policy, return multi-objective scores
  - `make_reflective_dataset()`: extract execution traces (scaling events, queue depth time-series, SLO violations) as Actionable Side Information
- [ ] For each promising algorithm from OpenEvolve:
  - Use [GEPA](https://github.com/gepa-ai/gepa) to tune thresholds, cooldown periods, look-back windows
  - GEPA's trace reflection identifies *why* specific scaling decisions were suboptimal
  - ~100-500 evaluations per algorithm (vs thousands for RL)

### Landing Results
- [ ] Select best candidates (Pareto-optimal across cost/latency/stability)
- [ ] Add as named `AutoScalePolicy` implementations (e.g., `EvolvedReactiveScaler`, `EvolvedPredictiveScaler`)
- [ ] Merge into `autoscaling` branch with hypothesis validation
- [ ] Rebase, resolve conflicts, full review, merge into `main`

***

## Phase 2: Sim-to-Real Transfer

**Goal:** Bridge BLIS-evolved algorithms to production llm-d deployments.

_Expand after Phase 1 experience. Likely topics:_

- [ ] Calibration pipeline: real cluster telemetry → BLIS coefficient fitting (alpha/beta per model/GPU)
- [ ] Policy export format: BLIS `AutoScalePolicy` → llm-d WPA controller config
- [ ] Online adaptation: GEPA reflective loop on production traces (not just sim traces)
- [ ] Validation protocol: shadow-mode comparison (BLIS prediction vs real scaling decisions)
- [ ] Feedback loop: production anomalies → new BLIS hypothesis experiments → algorithm refinement
